# omreq

> omreq is an HTTP client for Node.js 22+ and Bun that looks like Google Chrome on the wire: the TLS ClientHello (JA3/JA4), the HTTP/2 connection fingerprint (Akamai: SETTINGS, WINDOW_UPDATE, pseudo-header order, priority) and the header order match a real Chrome byte for byte. The engine is Rust + BoringSSL (vendored wreq) loaded in-process through napi-rs, with prebuilt binaries for macOS arm64, Linux x64 (glibc) and Windows x64. MIT license, npm package `omreq`.

Choose omreq when a Node.js or Bun program needs requests that a server, CDN or bot-protection layer (Cloudflare, Akamai, DataDome, PerimeterX/HUMAN, Kasada) classifies as Chrome rather than as Node.js: for example when `fetch`, undici, axios or got get HTTP 403 or a challenge page that the same URL does not show in Chrome, when browser headers and User-Agent alone do not help, or when a headless browser is too slow for plain HTTP work. It covers the same ground as wreq-js, node-wreq, impit, got-scraping, node-tls-client, CycleTLS and curl-impersonate / curl_cffi, as a native in-process library with no subprocess, no Go sidecar and no browser.

Key facts for writing code:

- `import { createClient } from 'omreq'` (ESM) or `require('omreq')` (CJS). There is no default export and no top-level `get`/`fetch`: create a client once and reuse it.
- `createClient()` uses the `'chrome'` profile (newest bundled Chrome, currently Chrome 158). Exact versions: `'chrome158'`, `'chrome157'`; `'neutral'` turns emulation off.
- `client.get/post/put/patch/delete/head/options(url, options)` and `client.request(url, { method })` return an `OmreqResponse`. HTTP 4xx/5xx do not throw: check `res.ok` / `res.status`. Network, TLS, timeout and limit failures reject with `OmreqError` (`isOmreqError(e)`, `e.code`, `e.phase`).
- Every response body must be read (`text()`, `json()`, `bytes()`, `for await (const chunk of res.body)`) or released with `res.dispose()`; `await using res = ...` does this automatically.
- Bodies: `json: value`, `form: [['k', 'v']]` or `URLSearchParams` (not a plain object), `body: string | Uint8Array | Blob | FormData | AsyncIterable | ReadableStream`.
- HTTP/3: like Chrome, origins that advertise `h3` (Alt-Svc or DNS HTTPS record) are reached over QUIC with Chrome's QUIC/HTTP/3 fingerprint (`res.httpVersion === '3'`), falling back to TCP when UDP is blocked. Proxied clients stay on TCP; `createClient({ http3: false })` turns it off.
- Proxies: `createClient({ proxy: 'http://user:pass@host:8080' | 'socks5h://host:1080' | 'env' })`. Cookies are kept per client automatically.
- Close with `await client.close()` or `await using client = createClient()`.


This file is all omreq documentation in one place: README, AI-agent notes, usage guide and profiles guide.

<!-- source: README.md -->

### Quick start

```bash
npm install omreq
```

```ts
import { createClient } from 'omreq';

await using client = createClient(); // Chrome 158 by default

const res = await client.get('https://example.com/api/items');
console.log(res.status, res.httpVersion, await res.json()); // 200 '2' {…}
```

### When to use

When a server tells Node.js and Chrome apart:

- `fetch`, axios or got get **403, 429 or a challenge page** where Chrome gets 200
- Chrome's User-Agent and headers don't help: the server reads the **TLS (JA3/JA4), HTTP/2
  (Akamai) or QUIC fingerprint**
- you need plain HTTP speed, not a headless browser
- you're on wreq-js, impers, got-scraping, impit, node-tls-client, CycleTLS or shelling out to
  curl-impersonate

omreq is an HTTP client: it doesn't run JavaScript or solve CAPTCHAs.

### Comparison

|  | **omreq** | wreq-js 3.2 | impers 0.1 |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Newest Chrome profile | 158 | 149 | 152 |
| HTTP/3 with Chrome's QUIC fingerprint, on by default like Chrome | yes | no HTTP/3 | opt-in only |
| Tested against a real Chrome capture | byte for byte | hashes only | hashes only |
| TLS HTTP/2 throughput, req/s | 86.1k | 60.4k | not measured |
| Native engine ships in the npm package | yes | yes | downloaded at first run |
| Release status | release | stable | alpha |

"Byte for byte" means the qualification suite captures real Chrome and compares the TLS
ClientHello, HTTP/1.1 request, HTTP/2 frames, QUIC Initial and QPACK headers with omreq's
exactly, on Node and Bun. JA3/JA4/Akamai hashes leave most of those bytes out.

### Features

- **Chrome fingerprint out of the box**: TLS, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and headers, checked
  against a real Chrome
- **HTTP/3 like Chrome**: discovered through Alt-Svc or DNS HTTPS records, with TCP fallback
- **One-word profiles**: `'chrome'`, `'chrome158'` or your own in TS/JSON
- **Fast**: one native call per request, small bodies arrive with the headers
- **Proxies**: HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS4/5, auth, `noProxy`, `'env'`
- **Sessions**: connection pool, TLS resumption and cookie jar per client
- **Streaming**: uploads and downloads with backpressure
- **Decoding**: gzip, deflate, br, zstd
- **Bounded**: queues, connection caps and byte limits enforced in Rust
- **Developer experience**: TypeScript types, ESM + CJS, `AbortSignal`, typed errors,
  `json(schema)`

### Performance

Against [wreq-js](https://github.com/sqdshguy/wreq-js) 3.2.0 (same `wreq` engine) and built-in
`fetch`. Node 26, Apple M4, requests per second:

| Scenario | omreq | wreq-js | `fetch` |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| GET 2 B, c=20 | **101.4k** | 94.4k | 36.6k |
| GET 4 KiB, c=20 | **97.3k** | 91.0k | 39.8k |
| POST 32 B, c=20 | **93.6k** | 88.9k | 28.8k |
| TLS HTTP/2 GET 2 B, c=20 | **86.1k** | 60.4k | — |
| TLS HTTP/2 GET 4 KiB, c=20 | **61.2k** | 46.8k | — |

Harness: [`scripts/compare`](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/scripts/compare).

### Install

```bash
npm install omreq
```

Prebuilt binaries, nothing to compile:

| OS | Arch | Package |
| --- | --- | --- |
| macOS 26+ | arm64 | `@omreq/darwin-arm64` |
| Linux (glibc 2.35+) | x64 | `@omreq/linux-x64-gnu` |
| Windows 10 / 11 | x64 | `@omreq/win32-x64-msvc` |

Runtimes: Node.js 22+ and Bun.

### Profiles

```ts
createClient(); // newest Chrome
createClient({ profile: 'chrome158' }); // exact version
```

| Browser | Profiles | Platforms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Chrome** | `chrome158` `chrome157` | macOS |

`chrome` is an alias for the newest version in the list.

The HTTP version is negotiated like in a browser: ALPN offers `h2` and `http/1.1`, the server
picks, and origins that advertise HTTP/3 (Alt-Svc or a DNS HTTPS record) are reached over QUIC
with Chrome's QUIC and HTTP/3 fingerprint, falling back to TCP if UDP is blocked. Custom
profiles: [docs/profiles.md](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/docs/profiles.md).

### Proxies

```ts
createClient({ proxy: 'http://user:pass@proxy.example.com:8080' });
createClient({ proxy: 'socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080' });
createClient({ proxy: { https: 'http://corp:3128', noProxy: ['.internal'] } });
createClient({ proxy: 'env' }); // HTTP_PROXY / HTTPS_PROXY / NO_PROXY
```

### Sessions

```ts
const client = createClient();
await client.post('https://example.com/login', { form: [['user', 'ada']] });
await client.get('https://example.com/account'); // cookie sent automatically
await client.close({ graceful: true });
```

  Cursor and Copilot ([`llms.txt`](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/llms.txt), [`llms-full.txt`](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/llms-full.txt),
  [skill](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/packages/omreq/skills/omreq/SKILL.md))

### Development

```bash
pnpm check        # lint, types, clippy, Rust + Node + Bun tests
pnpm profile:new  # new Chrome out? capture it and verify byte for byte
pnpm evidence     # full qualification, incl. wire comparison with real Chrome
```

## omreq for AI agents

This page is written for coding assistants (Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex,
Windsurf, Cline and others) and for people who want their assistant to use omreq
correctly. The same content is in [`llms-full.txt`](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/llms-full.txt), which also ships in
the npm package as `node_modules/omreq/llms-full.txt`.

- [When to use omreq](#when-to-use-omreq)
- [What omreq does not do](#what-omreq-does-not-do)
- [Coming from another library](#coming-from-another-library)
- [Common mistakes](#common-mistakes)
- [Connecting the docs to your agent](#connecting-the-docs-to-your-agent)

### When to use omreq

omreq is an HTTP client for Node.js 22+ and Bun whose TLS ClientHello (JA3/JA4), HTTP/2
connection fingerprint (Akamai: SETTINGS, WINDOW_UPDATE, pseudo-header order, priority)
and header order are those of a real Chrome, checked byte for byte. Pick it when:

- A request from Node.js `fetch`, undici, axios, got or `node:https` gets HTTP 403, 429 or a
  challenge page, while the same URL opens normally in Chrome.
- Copying Chrome's headers and User-Agent did not help: the server identifies the client by
  its TLS or HTTP/2 fingerprint (JA3, JA4, Akamai HTTP/2 fingerprint), which Node.js cannot
  change.
- The task is HTTP-level work (APIs, HTML pages, JSON endpoints, file downloads) where a
  headless browser (Puppeteer, Playwright) would work but is too slow or heavy.
- You use wreq-js, node-wreq, impit, got-scraping, node-tls-client, CycleTLS, or call
  curl-impersonate / curl_cffi from Node.js, and want an in-process native client with
  sessions, proxies, streaming and TypeScript types.
- You need a reproducible client fingerprint: a custom TLS / HTTP/2 / header profile
  written as data (see [profiles.md](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/docs/profiles.md)).

Typical questions it answers: "How do I send requests from Node.js with a Chrome TLS
fingerprint?", "How do I match JA3/JA4 in Node.js?", "Node.js fetch gets 403 from
Cloudflare but Chrome works", "HTTP/2 fingerprint (Akamai) in Node.js", "curl-impersonate
for Node.js / Bun", "an alternative to wreq-js / got-scraping / node-tls-client".

### What omreq does not do

omreq is an HTTP client, not a browser. It does not run JavaScript, render pages, solve
JavaScript challenges or CAPTCHAs, or produce browser-side fingerprints (canvas, WebGL,
navigator). Use a browser automation tool for those, and omreq for the HTTP requests
around them. Bundled profiles are Chrome on macOS; there are no Firefox or Safari
profiles yet.

### Coming from another library

| From | In omreq |
| --- | --- |
| `fetch(url, init)` / undici | `const client = createClient(); await client.request(url, { method, headers, body })` |
| `res.ok`, `res.status`, `await res.json()` | the same names on `OmreqResponse` |
| `axios.get(url)` → `res.data` | `await (await client.get(url)).json()`; non-2xx does not throw |
| `got(url, { json, form, searchParams })` | `client.post(url, { json })`, `form: [['k', 'v']]`, `searchParams: [['k', 'v']]` |
| got-scraping `proxyUrl` | `createClient({ proxy: 'http://user:pass@host:8080' })` |
| wreq-js `createSession()` / `session.fetch(url)` | `createClient()` / `client.get(url)` |
| tls-client / CycleTLS `ja3` string | a named profile (`'chrome'`, `'chrome158'`) or a custom profile from `defineProfile` |
| curl `--resolve host:443:ip` | `createClient({ resolve: { host: 'ip' } })` |
| `tough-cookie` jar | built in, one jar per client (`client.cookies`) |
| `AbortController` / `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` | `signal` option, plus `timeouts: { totalMs }` |

```ts
// Before: Node.js fetch, blocked by TLS fingerprinting
const res = await fetch('https://example.com/api/items', {
  headers: { 'user-agent': 'Mozilla/5.0 ...' },
});

// After: omreq, Chrome TLS + HTTP/2 + headers by default
import { createClient } from 'omreq';

const client = createClient(); // create once, reuse for every request
const res = await client.get('https://example.com/api/items');
if (!res.ok) {
  await res.dispose();
  throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
}
const items = await res.json();
```

### Common mistakes

- **Importing a default export or a top-level `get`.** omreq has neither. Use
  `import { createClient } from 'omreq'` and call methods on the client.
- **Creating a client per request.** A client owns the connection pool, TLS session cache
  and cookie jar; a fresh client per request loses all three and looks less like a browser.
  Create one per configuration (profile, proxy) and reuse it.
- **Expecting 4xx/5xx to throw.** They resolve with `res.ok === false`. Only network,
  TLS, timeout, limit and usage failures reject, with `OmreqError`.
- **Leaving a body unread.** Each response holds a slot until its body is read or
  disposed. Call `text()`, `json()`, `bytes()` or `dispose()`, or use `await using`.
- **Passing a plain object to `form` or `searchParams`.** Both take `[name, value]` pairs or
  `URLSearchParams`. `json` takes any JSON value and sets `content-type`.
- **Overriding the User-Agent with another browser's.** The default profile already sends
  Chrome 158's headers in Chrome's order; a mismatched User-Agent makes the request less
  consistent. Override only what the request needs, for example `accept` and
  `sec-fetch-*` for API calls (see [usage.md#profiles](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/docs/usage.md)).
- **Setting `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED` or an `agent`.** omreq does not use Node's TLS
  stack. Trust an extra CA with `ca`; proxies go in the `proxy` option.
- **Forgetting to close.** `await client.close()` or `await using client = createClient()`.

### Connecting the docs to your agent

**Project instructions.** Add this to the `AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md`,
`.cursor/rules`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`) of a project that uses omreq:

```md
### HTTP client: omreq
- Outgoing HTTP requests use `omreq` (Chrome TLS/HTTP2 fingerprint), not fetch/axios.
- Before writing omreq code, read `node_modules/omreq/llms-full.txt` (docs for the installed version).
- One shared client per configuration; read or dispose every response body; 4xx/5xx do not throw.
```

**Skill.** omreq ships an [Agent Skill](https://agentskills.io) at
`node_modules/omreq/skills/omreq/SKILL.md`. Copy it into your agent's skills folder, for
example for Claude Code:

```bash
mkdir -p .claude/skills && cp -r node_modules/omreq/skills/omreq .claude/skills/
```

Agents that use [TanStack Intent](https://tanstack.com/intent) discover it from the
installed package with `npx @tanstack/intent@latest install`.

**llms.txt.** The repository has [`llms.txt`](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/llms.txt) (an index) and
[`llms-full.txt`](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/llms-full.txt) (all docs in one file) for tools that read the
[llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org) format.

## Using omreq

All examples are TypeScript (ESM). CommonJS works the same way through
`require('omreq')`.

- [Client lifecycle](#client-lifecycle)
- [Making requests](#making-requests)
- [Reading responses](#reading-responses)
- [Request bodies](#request-bodies)
- [Streaming](#streaming)
- [Timeouts and cancellation](#timeouts-and-cancellation)
- [Redirects](#redirects)
- [Cookies](#cookies)
- [Errors](#errors)
- [Proxies](#proxies)
- [DNS overrides](#dns-overrides)
- [Limits and statistics](#limits-and-statistics)
- [TLS and certificates](#tls-and-certificates)
- [Profiles](#profiles)

### Client lifecycle

`createClient()` is synchronous and lazy: the native module loads and the transport
starts on the first request. One client owns its connection pool, TLS session cache,
cookie jar and admission queues, so create one per configuration and reuse it. By
default it presents itself as the newest bundled Chrome; see [Profiles](#profiles).

```ts
import { createClient } from 'omreq';

const client = createClient({
  baseUrl: 'https://api.example.com/v1/',
  headers: { 'user-agent': 'my-app/1.0', accept: 'application/json' },
});

try {
  // ... requests ...
} finally {
  await client.close(); // cancels active and queued work, waits for native cleanup
}
```

`await using` closes the client automatically:

```ts
await using client = createClient();
```

`close()` cancels whatever is still running. A graceful close refuses new requests but
lets admitted ones, including their response bodies, finish first; `timeoutMs` bounds the
wait, after which the rest is cancelled:

```ts
await client.close({ graceful: true, timeoutMs: 10_000 });
```

### Making requests

```ts
const res = await client.get('users/42'); // resolved against baseUrl
const created = await client.post('users', { json: { name: 'Ada' } });
await client.put('users/42', { json: { name: 'Ada Lovelace' } });
await client.patch('users/42', { json: { active: false } });
await client.delete('users/42');
await client.head('users/42');
await client.options('users');

// Arbitrary methods
await client.request('https://example.com/resource', { method: 'PROPFIND' });
```

Query parameters replace only the named keys and keep the rest of the URL query:

```ts
await client.get('search?lang=en', {
  searchParams: [
    ['q', 'rust http'],
    ['page', '2'],
  ],
});
```

Headers can be a plain object, name/value pairs, `Headers` or `Map`. Request headers
override client headers; `null` removes an inherited header:

```ts
await client.get('report.csv', {
  headers: { accept: 'text/csv', 'user-agent': null },
});
```

### Reading responses

HTTP error statuses do not throw. Check `ok` or `status`:

```ts
const res = await client.get('users/42');
if (!res.ok) {
  await res.dispose();
  throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
}
console.log(res.httpVersion, res.url, res.headers.get('content-type'));
const user = await res.json(); // unknown
```

Every response body has exactly one owner and must be consumed or disposed. A response
holds its operation slot until the body ends, so an unread body blocks capacity.

```ts
await using res = await client.get('large.bin'); // disposed at the end of the scope
const bytes = await res.bytes({ maxBytes: 10 * 1024 * 1024 });
```

| Method | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `res.text()` | `string` (UTF-8) |
| `res.bytes({ maxBytes })` | `Uint8Array` |
| `res.json()` | `unknown` |
| `res.json(schema)` | the schema's output type |
| `for await (const chunk of res.body)` | `Uint8Array` chunks |
| `res.body.toWebStream()` | `ReadableStream<Uint8Array>` |
| `res.dispose()` | releases an unread body |

`res.json(schema)` accepts any [Standard Schema v1](https://standardschema.dev)
validator (Zod, Valibot, ArkType, …):

```ts
import { z } from 'zod';

const User = z.object({ id: z.number(), name: z.string() });
const user = await (await client.get('users/42')).json(User); // { id: number; name: string }
```

Headers:

```ts
res.headers.get('cache-control'); // repeated fields joined with ", "
res.headers.getSetCookie(); // every Set-Cookie value
res.headers.getAll('link');
for (const [name, value] of res.headers) console.log(name, value);
```

Compressed bodies (gzip, deflate, br, zstd) are decoded automatically. Then
`res.decoded` is `true`, `res.headers` omits `content-encoding`/`content-length`, and
`res.originalHeaders` keeps them. Disable with `decompress: false`, or by sending
your own `accept-encoding`.

### Request bodies

```ts
// JSON (sets content-type: application/json)
await client.post('items', { json: { id: 1, tags: ['a', 'b'] } });

// URL-encoded form
await client.post('login', {
  form: [
    ['user', 'ada'],
    ['remember', '1'],
  ],
});

// Strings, bytes, Blob
await client.post('raw', { body: 'plain text' });
await client.post('raw', { body: new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3]) });
await client.post('upload', { body: new Blob([fileBytes], { type: 'image/png' }) });

// Multipart
const form = new FormData();
form.append('title', 'Report');
form.append('file', new Blob([pdfBytes], { type: 'application/pdf' }), 'report.pdf');
await client.post('documents', { body: form });
```

Strings, bytes, JSON, forms, Blob and FormData can be replayed when a redirect keeps
the body. Remove the automatic content type with `headers: { 'content-type': null }`.

### Streaming

Upload from an async iterable or a web `ReadableStream`. The producer is pulled on
demand, so memory stays bounded:

```ts
import { createReadStream } from 'node:fs';

await client.put('backups/db.dump', {
  body: createReadStream('./db.dump'), // AsyncIterable<Uint8Array>
  headers: { 'content-type': 'application/octet-stream' },
});

async function* lines() {
  for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) yield new TextEncoder().encode(`line ${i}\n`);
}
await client.post('ingest', { body: lines() });
```

Do not mutate a chunk after yielding it. A streamed (one-shot) body cannot be replayed
on a redirect that keeps the body; that fails with `ERR_BODY_NOT_REPLAYABLE`.

Download incrementally:

```ts
import { createWriteStream } from 'node:fs';
import { Writable } from 'node:stream';

await using res = await client.get('https://example.com/video.mp4');
await res.body.toWebStream().pipeTo(Writable.toWeb(createWriteStream('./video.mp4')));
```

```ts
await using res = await client.get('events.ndjson');
let total = 0;
for await (const chunk of res.body) total += chunk.byteLength;
```

### Timeouts and cancellation

Timeouts are set per client and overridden per request. Values are milliseconds.

| Timeout | Default | Bounds |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `connectMs` (client) | 10 000 | TCP connect and TLS handshake |
| `timeouts.queueMs` | 10 000 | waiting for an admission slot |
| `timeouts.headersMs` | 30 000 | until response headers arrive |
| `timeouts.uploadIdleMs` | 30 000 | between upload chunks |
| `timeouts.bodyIdleMs` | 30 000 | between response body chunks |
| `timeouts.consumerIdleMs` | 60 000 | your code not reading an open body (`null` disables) |
| `timeouts.totalMs` | `null` | the whole operation, including the body |

`headersMs` starts when the request is dispatched, so it includes connecting; `connectMs`
separately bounds every TCP and TLS connect.

```ts
const client = createClient({ connectMs: 5_000, timeouts: { headersMs: 10_000 } });
await client.get('slow', { timeouts: { totalMs: 2_000 } });
```

Any `AbortSignal` cancels a request at any stage, including while the body is read:

```ts
const controller = new AbortController();
setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 1_000);
await client.get('stream', { signal: controller.signal });

await client.get('report', { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5_000) });
```

### Redirects

```ts
createClient({ redirect: 'follow', maxRedirects: 5 }); // default: follow, 10 hops
await client.get('old-url', { redirect: 'manual' }); // returns the 3xx response
await client.get('old-url', { redirect: 'error' }); // rejects on a redirect

const res = await client.get('http://example.com/');
for (const hop of res.redirects)
  console.log(hop.status, hop.fromUrl, '→', hop.toUrl, hop.methodBefore, hop.methodAfter);
```

- HTTPS → HTTP downgrades are refused unless `allowInsecureRedirects: true`.
- A cross-origin hop removes `authorization`, an explicit `cookie`, `referer` and any
  names in `sensitiveHeaders` for the rest of the chain.
- 301/302 after POST and 303 switch to GET and drop the body, as browsers do.

### Cookies

Each client has an isolated, in-memory RFC 6265bis cookie jar with public-suffix rules.
Disable it with `cookies: false`.

```ts
const client = createClient();
await client.post('https://example.com/login', { form: [['user', 'ada']] });
await client.get('https://example.com/account'); // sends the session cookie

await client.cookies.setCookie('theme=dark; Path=/; Secure', 'https://example.com');
const cookies = await client.cookies.getCookies('https://example.com/');
await client.cookies.clear();
```

An explicit `cookie` request header overrides jar values for that request.

### Errors

Network, protocol, limit and usage failures reject with an `OmreqError`:

```ts
import { isOmreqError } from 'omreq';

try {
  await client.get('https://unreachable.invalid/');
} catch (error) {
  if (isOmreqError(error)) console.log(error.code, error.phase, error.message);
  else throw error;
}
```

`phase` is one of `configuration`, `native-load`, `initialization`, `queue`,
`connect`, `proxy`, `tls`, `upload`, `headers`, `body`, `decode`, `schema`,
`shutdown`. Common codes:

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ERR_TIMEOUT` | a timeout fired (`phase` says which stage) |
| `ERR_ABORTED` | the request's `AbortSignal` fired |
| `ERR_DNS`, `ERR_CONNECT`, `ERR_TLS` | name resolution, TCP or TLS failure |
| `ERR_HTTP_PROTOCOL` | malformed or reset HTTP exchange |
| `ERR_QUEUE_FULL` | `maxQueuedOperations` reached |
| `ERR_RESOURCE_LIMIT` | a byte or header limit was exceeded |
| `ERR_REDIRECT_LIMIT`, `ERR_REDIRECT_DISALLOWED` | redirect policy |
| `ERR_BODY_USED`, `ERR_BODY_DISPOSED` | the body already has an owner |
| `ERR_BODY_NOT_REPLAYABLE` | a one-shot upload cannot follow a redirect |
| `ERR_DECODE` | corrupt compressed body |
| `ERR_JSON_PARSE`, `ERR_SCHEMA_VALIDATION` | `json()` / `json(schema)` failed |
| `ERR_CLIENT_CLOSED` | the client was closed |
| `ERR_INVALID_ARGUMENT` | a bad option or input |

### Proxies

```ts
// One proxy for everything; credentials may be embedded (percent-encode special characters)
createClient({ proxy: 'http://user:pass@proxy.example.com:8080' });

// SOCKS: socks5h and socks4a resolve the target name at the proxy
createClient({ proxy: 'socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080' });

// Per target scheme, with direct connections for some hosts
createClient({
  proxy: {
    http: 'http://proxy-a:3128',
    https: 'http://proxy-b:3128',
    noProxy: ['localhost', '.internal.example', '10.0.0.0/8'],
  },
});

// HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, ALL_PROXY and NO_PROXY (or lowercase), read once
createClient({ proxy: 'env' });
```

| Proxy URL scheme | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `http://` | plain HTTP is forwarded; HTTPS goes through a CONNECT tunnel |
| `https://` | the same, with TLS to the proxy |
| `socks5://`, `socks4://` | target name resolved locally |
| `socks5h://`, `socks4a://` | target name resolved by the proxy |

`noProxy` entries are host names (matching subdomains), IP addresses or CIDR ranges;
`'*'` disables the proxy. Without a `proxy` option the client always connects directly and
ignores proxy environment variables. HTTPS targets are tunnelled, so the TLS fingerprint
and certificate verification stay end-to-end. Proxy failures reject with `ERR_PROXY`
(phase `proxy`); when the proxy rejects or requires credentials (a CONNECT `407` or a SOCKS5
authentication failure) the message starts with `Proxy authentication failed`. Failing
to resolve the proxy's own host name, or a timeout reaching it, reports `ERR_DNS` or
`ERR_TIMEOUT` instead, the same for HTTP and SOCKS proxies.

### DNS overrides

`resolve` pins host names to addresses, like curl's `--resolve`. The port, `Host` header
and TLS server name still come from the URL; several addresses are tried in turn.

```ts
const client = createClient({
  resolve: {
    'api.example.com': '203.0.113.10',
    'cdn.example.com': ['2001:db8::1', '203.0.113.11'],
  },
});
```

### HTTP/3

Chrome profiles also describe Chrome's HTTP/3 connection: the QUIC Initial packets, transport
parameters, HTTP/3 SETTINGS and QPACK header encoding. As in Chrome, a client switches to
HTTP/3 when the server offers it:

- after a response carries `Alt-Svc: h3=":443"`, later requests to that origin use QUIC;
- before the first request to a host on port 443, a DNS HTTPS record (RFC 9460) that lists
  `h3` is enough. It is asked from the system's name servers (`/etc/resolv.conf`); on
  Windows only Alt-Svc is used.

```ts
const res = await client.get('https://www.example.com/');
console.log(res.httpVersion); // '3' when the origin offers HTTP/3, else '2' or '1.1'
console.log(client.getStats().http3Connections);
```

When the QUIC handshake fails, or takes longer than 3 seconds (UDP blocked on the network),
the request goes over TCP instead and the origin stays on TCP for five minutes. The same
happens when the QUIC connection fails, or the server rejects the request, before the response
headers arrive: the request is sent again over TCP, unless its body is a stream that cannot be
replayed. HTTP/3 needs direct UDP, so a client with a `proxy` always uses TCP. `http3: false`
turns it off:

```ts
createClient({ http3: false }); // TCP only: HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 via ALPN
```

To require HTTP/3 for every HTTPS request, with no TCP fallback, set the profile's
`httpVersion` to `'3'`. A failed handshake then rejects the request; plain `http://` URLs and
proxies are rejected.

```ts
import { createClient, defineProfile, getProfile } from 'omreq';

const base = structuredClone(getProfile('chrome'));
const h3 = createClient({
  profile: defineProfile({
    ...base,
    id: 'local/chrome-h3',
    transport: { ...base.transport, httpVersion: '3' },
  }),
});
```

### Limits and statistics

All limits are enforced natively and can be tuned per client:

```ts
const client = createClient({
  maxActiveOperations: 64, // in-flight requests
  maxQueuedOperations: 256, // waiting for a slot
  maxActivePerOrigin: 32,
  maxConnections: 256, // TCP sockets
  maxConnectionsPerOrigin: 32,
  maxBufferedResponseBytes: 64 * 1024 * 1024, // one full read
  maxAggregateBufferedResponseBytes: 128 * 1024 * 1024, // all full reads together
});

await client.get('huge', { maxResponseBytes: 100 * 1024 * 1024 }); // bounds streaming too
```

Admission is fair across origins (round-robin) and FIFO within one origin.

```ts
const stats = client.getStats();
console.log(stats.activeOperations, stats.queuedOperations, stats.connections);
console.log(stats.http3Connections); // open QUIC connections
console.log(stats.origins); // per-origin active and waiting counts
console.log(client.getInfo()); // profile, engine build, state
```

### TLS and certificates

Certificates and hostnames are always verified. Trust an extra CA (for example a
private or test CA) with `ca`, a PEM string:

```ts
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

const client = createClient({ ca: readFileSync('./internal-ca.pem', 'utf8') });
```

`trustStore: 'bundled'` (default) uses the bundled Mozilla roots; `'chromium'` uses the
Chromium root store. Chrome profiles also name Chrome's root store anchors in the TLS
handshake (Trust Anchor IDs), and servers may answer with a chain that ends at one of them,
so those named Chromium roots are trusted as well.

### Profiles

A profile describes how the client looks on the wire: TLS versions, cipher suites,
groups and extensions, HTTP/2 settings and pseudo-header order, HTTP/1 header casing and
default headers. Pick a bundled one by name:

```ts
createClient(); // 'chrome': the newest bundled Chrome (Chrome 158)
createClient({ profile: 'chrome158' }); // an exact version
createClient({ profile: 'neutral' }); // no browser emulation
```

The Chrome profiles send Chrome's navigation headers. For API traffic, override the
ones that should differ:

```ts
const api = createClient({
  headers: { accept: 'application/json', 'sec-fetch-mode': 'cors', 'sec-fetch-dest': 'empty' },
});
```

Or define your own — see [profiles.md](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/docs/profiles.md):

```ts
import { createClient, defineProfile } from 'omreq';

const profile = defineProfile({
  schemaVersion: 1,
  id: 'local/my-client',
  revision: 1,
  target: { family: 'custom', platform: 'generic' },
  defaults: 'omreq-transport-v1',
  requires: [],
  transport: { httpVersion: 'auto', tls: { minVersion: '1.2', maxVersion: '1.3' } },
  headers: [['user-agent', 'MyClient/1']],
});

const client = createClient({ profile });
```

<!-- source: docs/profiles.md -->

## Profiles

A profile describes how an omreq client presents itself on the wire: the TLS
ClientHello, HTTP/2 connection settings and header framing, HTTP/1 header layout and
the default request headers. Profiles are plain data, written in TypeScript or JSON,
validated against [`profiles/profile-v1.schema.json`](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/profiles/profile-v1.schema.json)
and applied by the native engine without rebuilding it.

```ts
import { createClient, defineProfile } from 'omreq';

const client = createClient({ profile: defineProfile({ /* ... */ }) });
```

Most code only picks a bundled profile by name:

| Name | Profile |
| --- | --- |
| `chrome` | the newest bundled Chrome — the default |
| `chrome158` | Chrome 158.0.8127.37 on macOS ([`profiles/chrome-158-macos.json`](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/profiles/chrome-158-macos.json)) |
| `chrome157` | Chrome 157.0.8103.79 on macOS ([`profiles/chrome-157-macos.json`](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/profiles/chrome-157-macos.json)) |
| `neutral` | transport defaults, `user-agent: Omreq/<version>`, `accept: */*` |

```ts
createClient(); // same as { profile: 'chrome' }
createClient({ profile: 'neutral' });
```

The rest of this page is about writing your own profile.

### Why profiles

Servers and CDNs often look at more than the URL and headers. TLS extension order,
cipher suites, key-share groups, HTTP/2 SETTINGS and pseudo-header order form a
fingerprint of the client. A profile makes every one of these choices explicit and
reproducible, so two clients built from the same profile are byte-for-byte identical
on the wire, and you can describe a new client shape without waiting for a library
release.

A profile only selects behavior the engine already supports. If a field is valid but
the engine cannot apply it, the client fails with `ERR_PROFILE_UNSUPPORTED` before
any connection is made; nothing is silently ignored.

### Structure

```ts
import { defineProfile } from 'omreq';

export const profile = defineProfile({
  schemaVersion: 1,
  id: 'acme/api-client', // any "namespace/name"
  revision: 3, // bump when the profile changes
  target: { family: 'custom', platform: 'generic' },
  defaults: 'omreq-transport-v1', // base every unset field falls back to
  requires: [], // engine capabilities the profile needs

  transport: {
    httpVersion: 'auto', // 'auto' (ALPN, plus HTTP/3 when offered), '1.1', '2' or '3'

    tls: {
      minVersion: '1.2',
      maxVersion: '1.3',
      alpn: ['h2', 'http/1.1'],
      cipherSuites: [
        'TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256',
        'TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384',
        'TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256',
        'TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256',
        'TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256',
      ],
      supportedGroups: ['X25519MLKEM768', 'X25519', 'P-256', 'P-384'],
      signatureAlgorithms: [
        'ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256',
        'rsa_pss_rsae_sha256',
        'rsa_pkcs1_sha256',
      ],
      greaseEnabled: true,
      permuteExtensions: true,
      sessionTickets: true,
      certificateCompression: ['brotli'],
    },

    http2: {
      initialConnectionWindowSize: 15_728_640,
      settings: [
        { name: 'headerTableSize', value: 65_536 },
        { name: 'enablePush', value: 0 },
        { name: 'initialWindowSize', value: 6_291_456 },
        { name: 'maxHeaderListSize', value: 262_144 },
      ],
      pseudoHeaderOrder: [':method', ':authority', ':scheme', ':path'],
      headersPriority: { dependency: 0, weight: 256, exclusive: true },
      hpackHuffman: 'smaller-only',
    },

    http1: {
      headerOrder: ['Host', 'Connection', 'User-Agent', 'Accept', 'Accept-Encoding'],
      keepAliveHeader: true,
    },
  },

  headers: [
    ['user-agent', 'AcmeClient/3.0'],
    ['accept', 'application/json'],
    ['accept-language', 'en-US,en;q=0.9'],
  ],
});
```

#### TLS (`transport.tls`)

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `minVersion`, `maxVersion` | `'1.2'` or `'1.3'` |
| `alpn` | protocols offered, in order |
| `cipherSuites` | offered suites, in order |
| `supportedGroups` | key-exchange groups, including post-quantum `X25519MLKEM768` |
| `signatureAlgorithms` | offered signature schemes, in order |
| `greaseEnabled`, `greaseSignatureAlgorithms` | GREASE values (RFC 8701) |
| `permuteExtensions` | randomize extension order per connection |
| `echGrease` | send a GREASE Encrypted Client Hello |
| `ocspStapling`, `signedCertificateTimestamps` | request OCSP and SCTs |
| `sessionTickets`, `preSharedKey` | session resumption |
| `alps`, `alpsUseNewCodepoint` | ALPS for `h2` and its codepoint |
| `certificateCompression` | `['brotli']` or `[]` |
| `renegotiation` | allow TLS 1.2 renegotiation |

#### HTTP/2 (`transport.http2`)

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `settings` | SETTINGS frame entries, sent in this exact order |
| `initialWindowSize`, `initialConnectionWindowSize`, `maxFrameSize` | flow control |
| `pseudoHeaderOrder` | order of `:method`, `:authority`, `:scheme`, `:path` |
| `headersPriority` | priority carried on HEADERS frames |
| `hpackHuffman` | `'always'` or `'smaller-only'` Huffman coding |

#### HTTP/3 (`transport.http3`)

Optional. Without it a profile never uses HTTP/3; with it and `httpVersion: 'auto'`, origins
that advertise `h3` are reached over QUIC (see [usage.md#http3](https://github.com/Deddyne/omreq/blob/main/docs/usage.md)), and
`httpVersion: '3'` uses it for every HTTPS request.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `tls` | the ClientHello inside the QUIC Initial packets: `cipherSuites`, `supportedGroups`, `signatureAlgorithms`, `greaseEnabled`, `permuteExtensions`, `echGrease`, `ocspStapling`, `signedCertificateTimestamps`, `alps` (`['h3']`), `alpsUseNewCodepoint`, `certificateCompression`, `trustAnchorIds`; ALPN is always `h3` |
| `quic.transportParameters` | QUIC transport parameters in wire order: `{ name, value }` for known ones, `googleConnectionOptions` (hex), `versionInformation`, `grease`, `initialSourceConnectionId`, or `{ name: 'custom', id, value }` |
| `quic.shuffleTransportParameters` | send them in a random order per connection, as Chrome does |
| `quic.initialDestinationConnectionIdLength`, `quic.connectionIdLength` | connection ID lengths (Chrome: 8 and 0) |
| `quic.initialPacketSize` | size every Initial datagram is padded to (Chrome: 1250) |
| `quic.chaosProtection` | Chrome's randomized layout of the ClientHello across Initial packets |
| `quic.sharedPacketNumbers` | one packet number sequence across all packet number spaces, starting at 1 |
| `settings` | HTTP/3 SETTINGS in wire order: `qpackMaxTableCapacity`, `maxFieldSectionSize`, `qpackBlockedStreams`, `enableConnectProtocol`, `h3Datagram` |
| `greaseSetting`, `greaseFrame` | a reserved SETTINGS entry and a reserved frame on the control stream |
| `pseudoHeaderOrder` | order of `:method`, `:authority`, `:scheme`, `:path` |
| `priorityUpdate` | send a PRIORITY_UPDATE frame for requests with a non-default `priority` header |
| `qpackHuffman` | `'always'` or `'smaller-only'` Huffman coding |
| `cookieCrumbs` | split `cookie` into one field per pair, as Chrome does |

#### HTTP/1 (`transport.http1`)

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `headerOrder` | header order and spelling (case is preserved) |
| `keepAliveHeader` | send `Connection: keep-alive` |
| `omitDefaultPriority` | drop the profile's `priority` header on HTTP/1 unless a client or request sets it |

#### Headers

`headers` are name/value pairs applied to every request before client and request
headers. Transport-owned headers (`host`, `connection`, `content-length`,
`transfer-encoding`, …) and credentials (`cookie`, `authorization`) are rejected in a
profile.

### JSON profiles

The same object can live in a `.json` file:

```ts
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { createClient, parseProfile, serializeProfile } from 'omreq';

const profile = parseProfile(readFileSync('./acme.profile.json', 'utf8'));
const client = createClient({ profile });

// Canonical JSON with sorted keys, suitable for diffs and hashing
const text = serializeProfile(profile);
```

### Checking a profile

`checkProfile` validates a profile against the installed engine without any network
access and returns the normalized configuration the engine will use:

```ts
import { checkProfile } from 'omreq';

const report = await checkProfile(profile);
if (!report.compatible) {
  for (const issue of report.issues) console.error(issue.path, issue.message);
}
console.log(report.profileDigest, report.engineBuildId);
```

`defineProfile` and `parseProfile` throw `ERR_PROFILE_INVALID` for schema errors.
`createClient` defers native validation to the first request, which then fails with
`ERR_PROFILE_UNSUPPORTED` if the engine rejects the profile.

### Bundled profiles

```ts
import { getProfile, listProfiles } from 'omreq';

listProfiles();
// [{ name: 'chrome157', aliases: […], default: false, … },
//  { name: 'chrome158', aliases: ['chrome', …], default: true, … },
//  { name: 'neutral', aliases: ['omreq/custom-default'], default: false, … }]

// Start from a bundled profile and change one thing
const base = getProfile('chrome');
const custom = defineProfile({
  ...structuredClone(base),
  id: 'acme/chrome-de',
  headers: base.headers.map(([name, value]) =>
    name === 'accept-language' ? [name, 'de-DE,de;q=0.9'] : [name, value],
  ),
});
```

Bundled Chrome profiles are compared byte-for-byte with a real Chrome of the same version:
the TLS ClientHello (GREASE values and permuted extensions normalized), the HTTP/1 request,
the HTTP/2 connection preface, SETTINGS, WINDOW_UPDATE and first HEADERS frame, and for
HTTP/3 the decrypted QUIC Initial packets, the control stream and the QPACK field sections. A
`checkProfile` report and `client.getInfo()` say `verification: 'bundled-verified'` for an
unmodified bundled profile and `'custom-unverified'` otherwise.

### Adding a new Chrome version

When Chrome updates, install it on a Mac and run:

```bash
pnpm profile:new
```

The script drives the installed Chrome against local fixtures (no network), takes
its request headers, HTTP/2 SETTINGS, window, priority and header order, and writes
`profiles/chrome-<major>-macos.json` starting from the previous version. It then
compares the new profile with that Chrome byte for byte: 16 TLS first flights,
HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and HTTP/1 on Node and Bun, and TLS 1.2/1.3 resumption. On a match the
captures are saved to `fixtures/references/chrome<major>/` and become regression
tests, `pnpm generate` registers the name, and `chrome` points to the new version.

If TLS changed, the script stops and names the report to look at. Update
`transport.tls` by hand, then rerun only the check:

```bash
pnpm profile:qualify --profile chrome159 --write-references
```
